title: Forming ions
keyIdea: An ion is an atom that has lost or gained electrons, so its protons and electrons no longer balance. Metals lose their outer electrons and become positive ions; non-metals gain electrons and become negative ions. The group number predicts the charge: groups 1, 2 and 3 give 1+, 2+ and 3+; groups 5, 6 and 7 give 3−, 2− and 1−.

kid: An atom has the same number of protons and electrons. Each proton counts as plus one. Each electron counts as minus one. They cancel out, so the atom has no charge.
If an atom loses or gains electrons, the two numbers stop matching. Now it has a charge. We call it an ion.
Sodium has 11 protons and 11 electrons. It gives away 1 electron. Now there are 11 plus and only 10 minus. One plus is left over, so sodium becomes a plus ion, Na⁺.
Chlorine does the opposite. It takes 1 electron, so it has 18 minus and 17 plus. One minus is left over, so it is Cl⁻. Metals give electrons away. Non-metals take them in.
adult: An ion is a charged particle formed when an atom loses or gains electrons. The nucleus does not change, so the number of protons stays the same. The charge is protons minus electrons: fewer electrons than protons gives a positive ion, and more gives a negative ion.

Atoms lose or gain the smallest number of electrons that leaves a full outer shell. Metals in groups 1, 2 and 3 lose 1, 2 or 3 electrons and form 1+, 2+ and 3+ ions, such as Mg²⁺. Non-metals in groups 5, 6 and 7 gain 3, 2 or 1 and form 3−, 2− and 1− ions, such as O²⁻. Carbon and silicon, in group 4, usually share electrons instead.

When a metal reacts with a non-metal, electrons move from the metal atoms to the non-metal atoms. The ions then join in the ratio that makes the charges cancel. Magnesium chloride is MgCl₂ because one Mg²⁺ needs two Cl⁻ ions. To draw an ion, show its outer shell, put square brackets round it and write the charge at the top right, such as [Cl]⁻ with 8 outer electrons.

Common mistakes: giving a metal ion a negative charge because it lost something; writing the number of outer electrons as the charge, such as 6+ for oxygen; and thinking Na⁺ has turned into neon. It has the same electrons as neon, but it still has 11 protons, so it is still sodium.

familyTip: Use red counters for protons and blue counters for electrons. Lay out 12 of each for magnesium, then take 2 blue away. Ask: which colour is left over, and how many? That leftover is the charge, 2+.

worked.title: What ion does a magnesium atom form, and why?
steps: Magnesium has 12 protons and 12 electrons, arranged 2,8,2. It is in group 2, so it has 2 outer electrons.
Losing 2 electrons leaves 2,8, a full outer shell. Gaining 6 would also fill a shell, but that is far more work.
Now there are 12 protons and 10 electrons. 12 − 10 = 2 extra positive charges.
The ion is Mg²⁺. Draw it as the 2,8 shells inside square brackets, with 2+ at the top right.

practice.prompt: A magnesium atom (group 2) forms an ion. What happens?
choices: It loses 2 electrons and becomes Mg²⁺
It gains 2 electrons and becomes Mg²⁻
It loses 2 electrons and becomes Mg²⁻
practice.hint: Magnesium is a metal. Do metals give electrons away or take them in?
practice.explain: Magnesium loses its 2 outer electrons. It keeps 12 protons but has only 10 electrons, so it is 2+, Mg²⁺.

practice.prompt: A metal in group {g}, period {r}, has {=8*r-14+g} protons. It forms an ion. How many electrons does the ion have?
practice.hint: The group number tells you how many outer electrons it loses. Take that away from the {=8*r-14+g} electrons of the atom.
practice.explain: The atom has {=8*r-14+g} electrons and loses its {g} outer ones: {=8*r-14+g} − {g} = {=8*r-14} electrons. The ion is {g}+.

practice.prompt: A non-metal in group {g}, period {r}, has {=8*r-14+g} protons. It forms an ion. What is the size of its negative charge?
practice.hint: A group {g} atom has {g} outer electrons. How many gaps are left in a shell that holds 8?
practice.explain: It gains 8 − {g} = {=8-g} electrons. That gives {=8-g} more electrons than protons, so the charge is {=8-g}−.

practice.prompt: Calcium forms Ca²⁺ and chlorine forms Cl⁻. What is the formula of calcium chloride?
practice.hint: The charges must add up to zero. How many 1− ions cancel one 2+ ion?
practice.explain: One Ca²⁺ needs two Cl⁻ to cancel its charge: 2+ and 2 × 1− make 0. So the formula is CaCl₂.

practice.prompt: Which is the correct way to draw a chloride ion?
choices: [Cl]⁻ with 8 electrons in the outer shell
[Cl]⁺ with 8 electrons in the outer shell
Cl⁻ with 7 electrons in the outer shell and no brackets
practice.hint: Chlorine gained one electron. How many are in its outer shell now, and what sign is the charge?
practice.explain: Chlorine 2,8,7 gains one electron to reach 2,8,8. Draw the 8 outer electrons inside square brackets, with − at the top right.

pool.prompt: Potassium is in group 1. What is the charge on a potassium ion?
pool.hint: Group 1 atoms have one outer electron. Is it easier to lose 1 or gain 7?
pool.explain: Potassium loses its single outer electron. It then has one more proton than electrons, so the ion is K⁺, a 1+ charge.

pool.prompt: Why does a sodium ion have a positive charge?
choices: It lost an electron, so it has more protons than electrons
pool.hint: Which particles change when an ion forms: protons or electrons?
pool.explain: Only electrons move. Sodium loses one, leaving 11 protons and 10 electrons, so one positive charge is left over.

pool.prompt: An ion of an element in group {g} has {=8*r-14+g} protons and {=8*r-14} electrons. What is the size of the positive charge on the ion?
pool.explain: {=8*r-14+g} − {=8*r-14} = {g}. There are {g} more protons than electrons, so the ion has a charge of {g}+.

pool.prompt: A non-metal atom in group {g}, period {r}, has {=8*r-14+g} protons. How many electrons does its ion have?
pool.hint: Start with {=8*r-14+g} electrons, then add the number needed to fill a shell of 8 from {g}.
pool.explain: It gains 8 − {g} = {=8-g} electrons: {=8*r-14+g} + {=8-g} = {=8*r-6} electrons, a full outer shell.

pool.prompt: Aluminium forms Al³⁺ and oxygen forms O²⁻. What is the formula of aluminium oxide?
pool.hint: Find the smallest total positive charge that equals a total negative charge. Try 6.
pool.explain: Two Al³⁺ give 6+ and three O²⁻ give 6−. They cancel, so the formula is Al₂O₃.

pool.prompt: A sodium ion has the same electron arrangement as neon. Which statement is true?
choices: It is still sodium, because it has 11 protons
pool.hint: What decides which element an atom or ion belongs to?
pool.explain: The number of protons decides the element. Na⁺ has 11 protons and 10 electrons, while neon has 10 of each.

pool.prompt: Magnesium reacts with oxygen to form magnesium oxide. Which way do the electrons move?
choices: 2 electrons move from magnesium to oxygen
2 electrons move from oxygen to magnesium
No electrons move; they stay on each atom
pool.hint: Which one is the metal? Metals give electrons away.
pool.explain: Magnesium, the metal, gives its 2 outer electrons to oxygen. That makes Mg²⁺ and O²⁻, and the charges cancel: MgO.

pool.prompt: Oxygen is in group 6. Which ion does it form?
pool.hint: Six outer electrons: is it fewer moves to lose 6 or to gain 2?
pool.explain: Oxygen gains 2 electrons to fill its outer shell. It then has 2 more electrons than protons, so it is O²⁻.

visual.caption: Which ions do these elements form? Use the group number. Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: move electrons off and onto atoms, watch the charge ledger tip, pass electrons from magnesium to chlorine, then draw the ion.
